Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:41: And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Mechilta (Parashat Mishpatim) on the verse, "And you shall be men of holiness unto Me" (Exodus 22:30): Rabbi Yishmael said, when you are holy, behold, you are Mine — so far his words. He comes to explain the word "unto Me," which seems superfluous, saying that the verse means: when you become men of holiness, you are Mine — behold, you are Mine. The intent is that we have a fitting bond to become united together, as the verse says, "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 19:2), and as we elaborated above in the preceding chapter, that Israel need to be a fitting vessel to receive His holiness. And from the implication of a positive statement one may infer its negative: that if one does not sanctify himself, he is not His — for what bond does a physical person have to be joined with the spiritual and holy One, blessed and exalted be He, Master of all holinesses, unless he sanctifies himself and separates from the affairs of the world? He then remains physical, ruled over by mere doing, and behold, he belongs to another and is not His. For whatever a person sanctifies — even if it is only a small measure of holiness in the mystery of the nefesh — behold, it belongs to Him, blessed be He, in the mystery of oneness, as will be explained, please God; but if not, it belongs to another. Therefore let the living take this to heart, to sanctify himself and cleave to Him, blessed be He, as much as he is able.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:42: And with this, this chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:1: Having explained in the preceding chapter that a person is obligated to sanctify every single one of the six days of the week and to conduct himself with the holiness of the Sabbath day, it is fitting to explain what the forms of holiness are that one must practice on the day of Shabbat and on the other days.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:2: We shall say that although the forms of holiness found in the Torah and in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, are many, as will be explained, what is written regarding the day of Shabbat is three: first, holiness of thought; second, holiness of speech; third, holiness of labor — and these three are the main means for a person to cleave [to God].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:3: And even though eating is permitted on Shabbat, this does not undermine the [general] cancellation of holiness [from ordinary eating] on the six weekdays; even though a person eats on the six weekdays, if his eating is for the sake of Heaven, as will be explained, his eating will bring him to sanctify himself and cleave [to God]. Nevertheless, the eating of Shabbat is not like the eating of the other weekdays, for in the eating of Shabbat, "delight" (oneg) is mentioned, as it is written, "and call the Sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), and this is the mystery of [the acrostic] "Eden, river, garden," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:4: Likewise regarding the matter of marital relations on Sabbath night, which is elaborated in the Zohar (Parashat Yitro 89a), where it says that concerning it, "You shall be holy" is said; even if another person learns from the [manner of] relations found on Shabbat and applies it to the weekdays — if he sanctifies himself on the weekdays at midnight, as will be explained, in the manner of the union on Sabbath night — he has lost nothing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:5: The holiness of thought regarding Shabbat we find in the Mechilta (Parashat Yitro), in these words: "Six days shall you labor" (Exodus 20:9) — is it possible for a person to complete all his labor in six days? Rather, rest as though all your labor were done. Another interpretation: rest from thinking about labor — so far his words. It is thus made explicit that we were warned not to think about any matter of worldly affairs, so that our thought may remain attached to the Name, blessed be He, and to anything that is His service.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:6: Likewise regarding the holiness of speech, as the verse says, "from pursuing your affairs and speaking words [of idle chatter]" (Isaiah 58:13); and how much they elaborate in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 205b) about one who speaks mundane talk on Shabbat, that it is as if he desecrates the Sabbath — as we shall elaborate further below (ch. 14).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:7: The holiness of labor is explained in several verses in the Torah: "Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day there shall be to you a holy day, a Sabbath of solemn rest to the Lord" (Exodus 35:2), and likewise in the Ten Commandments, "Six days shall you labor and do [all your work], and the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:9-10). In saying "to the Lord your God," [the intent is] that you should think as though all your labor were done, and you have nothing of the affairs of this world, so that the whole day may be holy and you may cleave to the Lord your God. This is [the meaning of] "Shabbat shabbaton" — "Shabbat" in deed, "Shabbaton, holy" in thought.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:8: You already know that "holy" refers to the mystery of thought; therefore a person is obligated to sanctify his thought on the day of Shabbat and to separate it from all matters of the physicality of this world, for the whole reality of Shabbat is holy, and it is the mystery of the world of souls that opens on Shabbat, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah 136a): that the souls that are in the lower Garden of Eden ascend to the upper Garden of Eden, and supernal souls descend to crown Israel; and likewise souls that have been refined during the six weekdays enter the lower Garden of Eden. And it says: on Sabbath eve there is a circulation of souls (as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have taught us, as mentioned above) — these go and those come, these descend. Who has seen how many holy chariots roam here and there, all of them in joy, all encircling these souls, to crown the holy nation, to crown many righteous ones in the Garden of Eden below, until the hour that the herald stands and calls out, "Sanctified, sanctified" — then there is rest, a stilling of everything, and the wicked of Gehinnom are all quieted and given rest, and the souls are all crowned in their places, these above and these below. Fortunate is the people whose portion is this — so far his words. And so it further says there (95b): and on every Sabbath eve a person sits in the world of souls. And so it says in the Zohar (Parashat Emor 95a): on this day of Shabbat, all sorrow, all anger, and all distress are forgotten from the whole world, because it is the day of the King's wedding feast, when souls are increased, in the manner of the World to Come — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:9: Now since the day of Shabbat is holy because souls are increased on it, it is fitting to make it a principal matter to sanctify the added soul with its supernal holiness, in every kind of holiness — and holiness of thought is above them all, for it is the mystery of the additional soul that is added from above, from the place of holiness, as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Tzav 29a, Parashat Pinchas 242b-243a) — meaning that there is an added soul-portion for everyone, but each according to his own aspect: there is an added nefesh of several kinds, and there is an added ruach and an added neshamah — see there. Therefore the essential thing is that the additional soul should enjoy the intention of prayer and novel insights in Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:10: And it is likewise fitting for another reason: the "tabernacle of peace" spreads its wings over us, as is explained in Parashat Bereshit (Zohar 48a), and the verse says, "the burnt-offering of Shabbat on its Shabbat, in addition to the continual burnt-offering" (Numbers 28:10) — meaning that its ascent from Shabbat to Shabbat is greater than what ascends continually every day of the six days of the week, and this is "in addition to the continual burnt-offering." Therefore, in accordance with its refinement and ascent, one needs a greater refinement of thought and inner intention than on the other days.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:11: Regarding novel Torah insights, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach Lecha 173a), in these words: Come and see, when Shabbat enters, souls descend and rest upon the holy people, and the souls of the righteous ascend above; when Shabbat departs, the souls that rested upon Israel ascend, and the souls of the righteous descend. Once all the souls that rested upon Israel ascend, they stand in [their] image before the holy King; the Holy One, blessed be He, asks all of them, "What novel Torah insight did you say — this soul of so-and-so?" And all of them establish that matter in two academies, those below and the Holy One, blessed be He, above, confirming that matter. Come and see: when a matter is renewed in Torah, and the soul that descended on Shabbat occupies itself with those novel matters and ascends above, the whole entourage above listens to that matter, and the Holy Beasts grow in wings and are clothed in wings; and when the Holy One, blessed be He, asks and they [the souls] have nothing to answer and remain silent, then it is written of the Holy Beasts, "when they stood, they let down their wings" (Ezekiel 1:24), as it is said, "for they stood, they answered no more" (Job 32:16), and "and when he opened it, all the people stood" (Nehemiah 8:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:12: Further, they said in the Midrash Yalkut (Psalm 139, remez 888) on the verse "my unformed substance" (golmi): Rabbi Yehoshua says, they are three hundred sixty-five [days], and the unification of the world is one of them. Rabbi Levi said, this is Yom Kippur — "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a man to afflict his soul?" (Isaiah 58:5). Rabbi Yitzchak said, this is the day of Shabbat, as it is said, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (Exodus 20:8) — how does a person act? He does labor all six days and rests on the seventh, and reconciles with his children and household; and even so, though you do labor all six days, let the Sabbath day be devoted entirely to Torah. From here they said: a person should rise early and sit on the day of Shabbat and go to the synagogue and the study hall, and read in the Torah and study in the Prophets, and afterward go home and eat and drink, to fulfill what is said, "Go, eat your bread in joy" (Ecclesiastes 9:7) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:13: Further, in the Tanna Devei Eliyahu, quoted in Yalkut Parashat Va'etchanan (remez 830), in explanation of the verse, in these words: "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" — with what do you sanctify it? With reading [Scripture], with a [special] portion, with food and drink, and with clean clothing. Even though Rabbi Akiva said, "Make your Shabbat like a weekday rather than depend on others," one should take meat and not increase wine, as it is said, "Be not among winebibbers" (Proverbs 23:20) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:14: Now, having explained the holiness of Shabbat in a general way, it is fitting that on every single day one draw an influx of that holiness — each according to his ability, whether for a part of the day, or most of it, or sometimes all of it — namely, that he should cease from his labor and seclude himself to occupy himself with Torah, and empty his thought of worldly affairs; for it is not fitting for a person to occupy himself with labor all day, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Beshalach 63a), in this vein: those who do not believe in the Holy One, blessed be He, do not wish to consider His ways, and they wish to trouble themselves all day pursuing sustenance, day and night, lest a piece of bread not come into their hands — who causes this to them? Because they are not people of faith — so far his words. Therefore it is fitting for a person to make his Torah study fixed and his labor occasional, as they said in tractate Avot (4:10): Rabbi Meir says, minimize your business dealings and occupy yourself with Torah; and if you neglect Torah you will have many neglecters [i.e., excuses] and so on. And this applies not only to Torah study but to every matter of a commandment and acts of kindness and the like, as Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar (Gate 2, sixth quality) regarding love: that one of the signs of love is that a person should not let any of his own affairs take precedence over the affairs of God, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:15: Further, they said in the Midrash Ruth (Midrash Zuta 1:20) that a certain pious man was extremely poor, and Elijah appeared to him in the guise of an Arab and gave him two coins; he traded with them and grew wealthy, and through his trading and dealings he forgot his set time of piety and the practice of his prayer. Elijah returned to him and took back from him the two coins he had given him, and his wealth declined, and that money was lost. The pious man returned to weeping, and so on; Elijah returned to him and said, "I swear to you that I will return to you those two coins, if you will keep your set time of piety and the practice of your prayer." He said to him, "Yes," and he took the two coins and traded with them and grew wealthy. This teaches that a person should not abandon his set time of piety for the sake of preoccupation with wealth. The reason is as explained, that one is obligated to make holy out of the mundane.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:16: And in the Mechilta (Parashat Ki Tisa) our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said: "Six days shall work be done" (Exodus 35:2), yet one verse says, "Six days shall you labor and do all your work" (Exodus 20:9) — how can these two verses be reconciled? Rather, when Israel do the will of the Omnipresent, their labor is done by others, as it says "work shall be done" [passive]; and so it says, "and strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners shall be your plowmen and vinedressers" (Isaiah 61:5). And when they do not do the will of the Omnipresent, their labor is done by themselves, as it says "and do all your work"; and not only that, but "and you shall serve your enemies whom the Lord will send against you" (Deuteronomy 28:48) — so far his words. And a similar thing is brought there in Parashat Vayakhel on the verse, "Six days shall work be done" (Exodus 35:2). This teaches that man was not created to occupy himself with physical labors that would nullify him from the study of Torah, but rather that all his days should be like Shabbat, occupied with Torah, and that strangers would stand to do his labor — this being when Israel do the will of the Omnipresent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:17: One must examine this carefully, for we find several pious men in the Talmud who were occupied with their labor and also occupied with Torah — such as Hillel and his colleagues — so why was their labor not done by others? One could resolve this, though somewhat forced, by saying that the passage speaks only in general terms of when Israel [as a whole] do the will of the Omnipresent, and so on; nevertheless the question remains, why does not every proper person merit this?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:18: One might say that there are two other aspects to this, besides what is stated in the first passage, for we find a parallel to this matter already among the early pious ones (chasidim rishonim), as it is said in tractate Berachot (5:1) that the early pious ones would tarry an hour before prayer, an hour after prayer, and an hour during prayer — three hours — and so for each of the three prayers, morning, afternoon, and evening. And they asked in the Gemara (32b, and see Yerushalmi 5:1): when was their Torah study and their labor done? And they answered: since they were pious, their Torah study was blessed and their labor was done by itself. It follows that of these too it is said, "work shall be done" [passive] — meaning that they begin some of the labor themselves, and blessing and success are found in that labor. But this is not quite the same as when all of Israel do the will of the Omnipresent, for the merit of the many is greater, and all their labor is done by others; whereas when they do not do the will of the Omnipresent, "do all your work" applies — that through themselves alone they must do all their labor.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:19: The second aspect, which is not quite as [elevated] as the early pious ones, concerns the Tannaim and Amoraim who occupied themselves part of the day with their labor; however, their labor was done through their outer, visible limbs, while their thought and soul remained attached to the Lord, blessed be He, and to His Torah. Let this not seem strange to you, for it is written in the Sefer Ma'aseh HaChasidim, found in a manuscript, that a certain pious ascetic who withdrew from the world, of those secluded ones who separate from worldly matters, was always attached to the Lord, blessed be He; and as time went by, this pious man came to a settled community, and they did not recognize him, and they made him the caretaker (shamash) of the synagogue; and when he would pour oil into the lamps, he would spill the oil outside, because from the greatness of his attachment [to God] he was unable to focus on pouring the oil into the lamps. The sage of the community understood the matter and said, "This caretaker deserves to be the sage in my place, and I will serve under him." Concerning something like this it is said, "Be you ravished always with her love" (Proverbs 5:19) — for from the greatness of one's love for Torah and attachment to it, one may err in the matters of this world. It follows that if their soul had always been sanctified with the holiness of Shabbat, which is the world of thought, as explained above [it would be different]. But when it is not fitting for him to be occupied with Torah [alone], his body and soul are entirely subjugated to labor.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:20: In our time, when Torah scholars do not occupy themselves with labor, and they are supported by the wealthy of the generation, they have a basis on which to rely, namely what is said in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Tzav 29a): that Torah scholars, who are called "sons," serve without accepting a reward — for on the weekdays they possess the soul-level of Atzilut, which is what the rest of the people, who serve in order to receive a reward, merit only on the day of Shabbat; for on the weekdays [ordinary people] have only the spirit of Metatron. These Torah scholars are called "Shabbat" even on the weekdays, for their only labor is the yoke of Torah and commandments; upon the common people (amei ha'aretz) falls the duty to feed and support them. And it says: whoever does not occupy himself with Torah and commandments has upon him the yoke of the kingdoms of the nations; whoever occupies himself with Torah and commandments has upon him the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, which is the final Heh, called the Kingdom of Heaven — it is certainly a yoke of a kingdom, because through her all the creatures of heaven and earth were created; this is what is written, "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created [behibar'am]" (Genesis 2:4) — "through the letter Heh He created them." And when the Sabbaths and festivals come, Binah, which is Yod-Heh-Vav, descends upon the [final] Heh, which is the Kingdom of Heaven — an additional soul — and it is "engraved upon the tablets" (Exodus 32:16), [namely] "I am [the Lord]" of the Exodus from Egypt, and she spreads her wings over her "daughter" and over her camps, and they have rest. And it further says: Torah scholars have nothing of their own; and if a common person supports him with his money and treats him according to his wish, to serve him, to conduct himself with the commandments as he wishes, there will be fulfilled in him "man and beast You save, O Lord" (Psalms 36:7) — He saves him from robbery and plunder, He saves him from the Attribute of Judgment so that it does not rule over him, and does not slaughter him with a defective knife, of which it is said, "You shall cast it to the dogs" (Exodus 22:30) — that is, Samael. And the soul of a Torah scholar is called "Shabbat the Queen," an additional soul, and so on. And it further says there: they, the Torah scholars, are the children of the King and the Matronita (Queen), and are called "Sabbaths and festivals," and have nothing of their own, for they are not people of labor like other servants, children of the mundane; their reward, in this world and in the World to Come, is to give them delight with every kind of food and drink, and to honor them with fine garments, in the manner of what is said of Shabbat, "honor it with clean clothing" — all that a person does for Sabbaths and festivals should be done for them, and whoever desecrates them is liable to stoning. So too, whoever makes improper use of a Torah crown is regarded like one who exchanges it, and so too one who makes [improper] use of one who studies halachot desecrates his Torah — and all the more so, one who demeans him, as if he demeans Sabbaths and festivals; and the masters of the Mishnah established, "Whoever demeans the festivals is as though he denies the fundamental principle [of faith]." And just as all the vessels of the Temple are called "holy," so too all who attend upon Torah scholars are called "holy," and the disciples of a master, who correspond to the limbs of his body, are called "holy of holies"; and the mystery of the matter is alluded to in "and the curtain shall divide unto you between the holy and the holy of holies" (Exodus 26:33) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:21: Thus a Torah scholar whose Torah study is his craft, and who does not occupy himself with labor, and has nothing with which to support himself, is permitted to benefit [from others' support], for he is holy Shabbat, sanctified even on the weekdays with the holiness of Shabbat. Such a Torah scholar, who does not occupy himself with labor at all, must without doubt sanctify his speech on the weekdays like his speech on Shabbat, and must likewise sanctify his thought, as explained above, and the other forms of holiness that will be explained, please God.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:22: For this reason, Rashbi, peace be upon him, who sanctified himself on the weekdays with the full holiness of the day of Shabbat, was called "Shabbat" by his colleagues. In these words, at the end of the Idra Nasso (144b): Rabbi Abba said, we are the six lamps that shine from the seventh; you are the seventh of all, for the six have no permanence except through the seventh, since everything depends on the seventh. Rabbi Yehudah called him "Shabbat of them all," as it is written, "Shabbat unto the Lord," "Holy unto the Lord" — just as Shabbat is unto the Lord, holy, so too Rabbi Shimon is "Shabbat unto the Lord, holy" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:23: And if he is occupied with labor, he must sanctify a part of the day from occupation with labor, and likewise sanctify his thought, speech, and other senses, as will be explained, please God; and at the very least, during the time of prayer, when he is free from labor whether he likes it or not, he should sanctify his thought from worldly affairs, so that that hour or half-hour will be holy with the holiness of Shabbat, and he should not interrupt his prayer with speech at all — so that no day be entirely devoid of the holiness of Shabbat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 3:24: And with this, this chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:1: Since our statement in the preceding chapter preceded, that the holiness of Shabbat is comprised of three things — thought, speech, and deed — we saw fit to follow it in this chapter by explaining what is found alluded to regarding this matter in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, and in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:2: The three things mentioned regarding holiness, Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (end of Tikkun 22, 68b), are neshamah, ruach, nefesh: thought corresponds to the neshamah, speech to the ruach, deed to the nefesh. In these words: the four elements of the body, in which YHVH dwells — this is "all that is called by My name, and for My glory I created it, I formed it, indeed I made it" (Isaiah 43:7). "I created it" — this is the holy neshamah, which is the world of thought. "I formed it" — this is the speaking spirit (ruach mamlela), from which the speaking living creatures come. "I made it" — this is the nefesh, in which there is deed, dwelling in the two hundred forty-eight commandments — so far his words. It follows that His intent, blessed be He, is to sanctify us with these three mentioned holinesses, so that we sanctify our nefesh, ruach, and neshamah with the holiness of Atzilut that flows into all the worlds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:3: This is [the meaning of] "and you shall sanctify yourselves... for I the Lord am your God" (Leviticus 20:7), and likewise "You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy" (Leviticus 19:2). These three words, "I the Lord your God," correspond to nefesh, ruach, neshamah, and the intent is that from Him, blessed be He, comes the flow of the nefesh, the ruach, and the neshamah, and all three of these aspects are holinesses by which they cleave to Him and He to them. The reason it says, in the term corresponding to the neshamah, "your God," is that a person's attachment to Him, blessed be He, is only through the neshamah, which is from the world of thought; and when he merits the supernal neshamah, then he is attached to his Creator, and then the Holy One, blessed be He, is designated as being his God, and the Shechinah rests upon him. This is true in every place mentioned in Parashat Kedoshim, "I the Lord your God," meaning that the three attributes mentioned, which comprise all of the ten [sefirot], dwell upon the neshamah that fulfills the commandments. Therefore, at the beginning of Parashat Kedoshim it says, "You shall be holy, for I am holy" — meaning, just as I am holy, so shall you be holy — the intent being for a person to sanctify himself, in nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, through the commandments and Torah, and by refining his thoughts and intentions; and by this, "I the Lord your God" — meaning that the attributes mentioned dwell within you. This is what was explained in the first chapter — that the souls must be a ready vessel to receive His holiness, as explained in the passage from Tanchuma at the beginning of that chapter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:4: These three flow into Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, as will be further explained below, please God. Corresponding to these three worlds — Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah — is what the Torah commanded, "And you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy." And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Balak 190b), in these words: The supernal praise that was not entrusted to the supernal angels alone, but to Israel — who is this? Holiness. Blessing was entrusted to them [the angels] alone, as it was entrusted to Israel; but holiness was not entrusted to them alone, only together with Israel, for they do not sanctify holiness except together with Israel. And should you say, but is it not written, "and one called to another and said" (Isaiah 6:3)? [The answer is:] when? At the time when Israel sanctify below; and until Israel sanctify below, they [the angels] do not say the Kedushah, because holiness ascends from three worlds and not from two. This is [the meaning of] "and called" — that is one; "to another" — two; "and said" — behold, three. There are three worlds, corresponding to which are three sanctifications; and therefore the praise is Israel's, for they bring up holiness below. Rabbi Elazar said, so it is, and we have established these matters; and we have further established that three holinesses were entrusted to Israel below, from this verse: "And you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I the Lord am holy" — "and you shall sanctify yourselves" is one, "and be holy" is two, "for I am holy" — behold, three. Here are three holinesses — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:5: It must be said that these three holinesses are in the places mentioned, because above this it says that Israel take up deed (asiyah) below from the time of the giving of the Torah onward, when they said, "We will do and we will hear" (Exodus 24:7) — this is "mighty in strength, who do His word" (Psalms 103:20), and so on. Therefore holiness ascends only from three worlds — that is, when Israel, who are in Asiyah below, join together with the angels, who are in Yetzirah — this is "one to another," "and said" — everything ascends and is elevated and joins with Beriah, "Holy, holy, holy," which is in Atzilut. This is "and you shall sanctify yourselves," and this is [also] "I the Lord" — for "holy" is in Beriah, "I the Lord" is in Atzilut, that first Being (havayah) which He and His life-force are one within — from which flows the sustenance of all holinesses, as explained; and this is [the meaning of] "I the Lord your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:6: Should you ask, why are not four holinesses mentioned, with a fourth holiness corresponding to Atzilut? One might say that because of the fineness and concealment of Atzilut, which is the mystery of concealed thought, we have no power to make ourselves a chariot for it; and behold, even Beriah is [called] thought, all the more so Atzilut. And because Beriah is [likewise] thought, the verse does not mention regarding it an action preparing for holiness, as it mentioned for the two preceding [worlds] — "and you shall sanctify yourselves," "and be holy" — but regarding the third it says "for I am holy," [meaning] I am holy of Myself. And since the lower Throne is [made] of Asiyah and Yetzirah prepared, corresponding to nefesh and ruach, the holiness of the neshamah, which is thought, rests of itself; and Atzilut is united with Beriah, for Rashbi, peace be upon him, called Beriah "the garments of Shabbat and Yom Tov" in the Tikkunim (3b), since the light of Atzilut, because of its concealment, cannot be revealed to us except through Beriah. Therefore between Beriah and Atzilut the verse does not mention a fourth holiness, but rather "for I am holy" in Beriah, "I the Lord," which is Atzilut clothed within it — and it is all one unity.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:7: We thus learn that a person cannot sanctify his thought to be attached to the Name, blessed be He, except through the neshamah that comes to him from the world of thought, as explained above; and the neshamah will not rest [upon him] unless its "throne" — that is, the nefesh and ruach — is rectified. For this, one must rectify his nefesh through the full perfection of performing the commandments, and sanctify himself from doing labor, which is in Asiyah, and sanctify all the vessels of his limbs by which deeds are done; and afterward sanctify [that which is] corresponding to the ruach; and once this is rectified, the supernal neshamah rests upon him, and behold he is holy, attached to Him, blessed be He. Nevertheless, even the neshamah does not rest of itself except through acquiring it by one's deeds and Torah study, as is explained at the beginning of Parashat Mishpatim (94b), which says: whoever merits more, they give him a neshamah from the side of the Throne. However, even if one prepares the groundwork to acquire them, the neshamah will not rest upon him if its "throne" — the nefesh and ruach — is not rectified as it should be.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:8: And in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra 25a), it is explained that whoever merits the neshamah, his soul ascends above every night into the world of souls, and he is attached and bound in the bundle of life more than one who merits only the ruach; for through the acquisition of the ruach he ascends only to the world of angels. In these words: once he acquires the ruach, that ruach goes forth, breaking through mountains and boulders, ascends and spreads out and enters among the supernal holy angels, and there it knows what it knows and learns matters, and returns to its place — this is the bond of a person with holiness, until he merits the neshamah and acquires it. Once he acquires the neshamah, it ascends higher and higher, and the guardians of the gates do not hinder it, and it goes and spreads out among those righteous ones who are bound in the bundle of life, and there it beholds the delight of the King and enjoys the supernal splendor — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:9: Further, confirmation for the reality of these three holinesses is found in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in Yoma (39a), in these words: our Rabbis taught, "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy" (Leviticus 11:44) — if a person sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him a great deal; if from below, they sanctify him from above; in this world, they sanctify him for the World to Come — so far their words. And just before this, adjacent to it, they say there, in these words: our Rabbis taught, "do not defile yourselves through them" (Leviticus 11:43) — if a person defiles himself a little, they defile him a great deal; if from below, they defile him from above; in this world, they defile him for the World to Come — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:10: Now, in light of the introduction we have given regarding the holinesses mentioned, one might say that this is the intent of the author of this passage regarding the three divisions — "sanctifies himself a little," "from below," "in this world" — which correspond to Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah, from below to above. And this is explained as it is explained in the Tikkunim (beginning of 23a): that the supernal Imma nests in the Throne with the three supernal sefirot, the middle pillar, comprising six sefirot, nests within Metatron, and the lower Imma nests within the Ofan (wheel), of which it is said, "and behold one wheel upon the earth" (Ezekiel 1:15) — so far his words. And the intent is that in accordance with how much a person sanctifies himself in the lower levels, holiness is bestowed upon him from the supernal levels in Atzilut; and this is [the meaning of] "for I the Lord your God am holy," as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:11: How so? "He sanctifies himself a little" — that is, the holiness of Asiyah, which is the Ofan — "they sanctify him a great deal," because the branch arouses the supernal root that is in Atzilut, and the Shechinah, who is [called] "Ani" (I), nests within the Ofan, bestowing there from her holiness, which is a great deal in comparison to the small branch, which is the Ofan. And further, regarding the Shechinah, the matter of multiplicity is fitting, as it is said, "How many are Your works, O Lord! In wisdom You have made them all" (Psalms 104:24) — meaning, through Mah, which is the Shechinah, "how many are Your works." And likewise in the palace of "sapphire brick," which corresponds to the Shechinah, we say in [the blessing] Yotzer Or, "Mah, how many are Your works, O Lord," as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar Parashat Pekudei 260b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:12: "From below," "they sanctify him from above" — the intent is that he further sanctifies himself in [the sphere of] Metatron, who is below, designated by the term "below" as explained in the Tikkunim (4a) and Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 228b), that Metatron is the horse upon which Tiferet rides; and just as the horse is below and the rider is above him, so it is with Metatron. In these words (Ra'aya Meheimna, ibid.): Metatron is the horse of Tiferet, in which all the sefirot are clothed, and this is like a body to a soul — so far his words. And "they sanctify him from above" means that Tiferet, which is YHVH, will shine within Metatron, like a soul within a body.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:13: "In this world," "they sanctify him for the World to Come" — this is the third holiness, that of Beriah, which is called "this world," for everything below the Shechinah is called "this world," just as she herself is called "this world," as in the matter of "when they were created (behibar'am)" — [read as] "He created them with Heh" (Menachot 29b), for through the final Heh came the creation of all the lower [worlds]. And "they sanctify him for the World to Come" is the shining of the supernal Imma, called "your God," with the three supernal sefirot that nest in the Throne. This is one approach to this passage, according to the introduction we gave.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 4:14: Regarding impurity, which explained three levels within it, these too follow this same pattern, except that where it says "they defile him a great deal," "from above," "for the World to Come," the intent is that they defile [i.e., close off] the flow so that it will not be bestowed below in Beriah-Yetzirah-Asiyah. For the three levels mentioned in the passage regarding impurity are based on the verse, "do not defile yourselves through them, lest you become impure through them (unetmetem bam)" (Leviticus 11:43), and they expounded in Yoma (39b) that "unetmetem" is a term of tamtum (dulling/stopping up), and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said: it was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael, [this] dulls a person's heart, as it is said, "do not defile yourselves through them, lest you become impure (unetmetem) through them" — do not read it "unetmetem" but "unitamtem" (and you become dulled) — so far his words.
